stem: A man of blood group A (genotype $I^Ai$) marries a woman of blood group B ($I^Bi$). Which blood groups are possible in their children?
hint: Each parent gives one of two alleles.
model_answer: **(c).** Gametes $I^A$, $i$ × $I^B$, $i$ give $I^AI^B$ (AB), $I^Ai$ (A), $I^Bi$ (B), $ii$ (O).

stem: In which organism does the female decide the sex of the offspring?
hint: Female heterogamety.
model_answer: **(c) Birds.** Females are ZW and make Z or W eggs; males are ZZ.

hint: Count heterozygous pairs only.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

label: PYQ-style
stem: Differentiate between incomplete dominance and co-dominance with one example each.
hint: Blend vs both shown.
model_answer:
*How much to write: a two-column table or 4 lines · 3 minutes*

| Incomplete dominance | Co-dominance |
|---|---|
| the F1 (heterozygote) shows a phenotype <mark>intermediate between the two parents</mark> | <mark>both alleles are fully expressed</mark> in the heterozygote |
| neither allele is completely dominant | each allele shows its own effect side by side |
| e.g. <u>snapdragon</u>: red (RR) × white (rr) → pink (Rr) | e.g. <u>ABO blood group AB</u>: $I^AI^B$ makes both A and B sugars |

:::tip Your answer must contain
- incomplete dominance = <mark>intermediate</mark> phenotype, with snapdragon
- co-dominance = <mark>both expressed</mark>, with blood group AB
:::

**Marks are lost for:** giving blood group AB as incomplete dominance; examples without the genotype.

scheme.step: Incomplete dominance: intermediate phenotype + snapdragon example
Co-dominance: both expressed + AB blood group example

label: PYQ-style
stem: Explain the molecular basis of sickle-cell anaemia.
hint: One base, one amino acid, one position.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 3–4 lines · 3 minutes*

- Sickle-cell anaemia is an <u>autosomal recessive</u> disorder; only <u>$Hb^SHb^S$</u> individuals show the disease.
- It is caused by a <u>point mutation</u> in the β-globin gene: the codon <mark>GAG changes to GUG</mark>.
- As a result, <mark>glutamic acid (Glu) is replaced by valine (Val) at the sixth position</mark> of the β-globin chain.
- The mutant haemoglobin <u>polymerises under low oxygen tension</u>, so the red blood cells change from biconcave discs to elongated <u>sickle-shaped</u> cells.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- <mark>GAG → GUG</mark> (single base change)
- <mark>Glu → Val at position 6</mark> of β-globin
- polymerisation at low O₂ → sickle cells
:::

**Marks are lost for:** writing the change as Val → Glu; saying the α chain is changed.

scheme.step: GAG → GUG; Glu → Val at position 6 of β-globin
Haemoglobin polymerises at low O₂ → sickle cells; autosomal recessive

label: PYQ-style
stem: A woman whose father was haemophilic marries a normal man. Work out, with a cross, the chance that (a) their son and (b) their daughter will be haemophilic.
hint: Her father gave her $X^h$.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 5–6 lines with a cross · 5 minutes*

Haemophilia is <u>X-linked recessive</u>. The woman got $X^h$ from her haemophilic father, so she is a <mark>carrier, $X^hX$</mark>; the man is normal, $XY$.

**Cross:** $X^hX \times XY$

$$\begin{array}{c|cc}♀\backslash♂ & X & Y\\\hline X^h & X^hX & X^hY\\ X & XX & XY\end{array}$$

$X^hX$ = carrier daughter; $XX$ = normal daughter; $X^hY$ = haemophilic son; $XY$ = normal son.

**(a)** Chance that a son is haemophilic: <mark>50%</mark>.
**(b)** Chance that a daughter is haemophilic: <mark>0%</mark> (but 50% of daughters are carriers).

:::tip Your answer must contain
- woman <u>carrier $X^hX$</u>, with the reason
- the cross with all four children
- <mark>sons 50%</mark>, <mark>daughters 0%</mark> (50% carriers)
:::

**Marks are lost for:** writing the woman as $X^hX^h$; giving 25% for sons by counting all children.

scheme.step: Sons 50% affected; daughters none affected, 50% carriers

label: PYQ-style
stem: *In Drosophila, a cross was made for two X-linked genes. For eye colour and body colour, only about 1.3% of the F2 flies showed new (non-parental) combinations; for eye colour and wing size, about 37.2% did.*

parts.stem: Name the phenomenon that makes parental combinations more frequent than expected.
parts.model_answer: Linkage (genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together).

parts.stem: Which pair of genes is more tightly linked? Give a reason.
parts.model_answer: Eye colour and body colour, because their recombination frequency (1.3%) is much lower.

scheme.step: Eye and body colour; lower recombination

parts.stem: How did Sturtevant use such data? Give two reasons why Drosophila suits genetic studies.
parts.model_answer: He used recombination frequency as a measure of distance between genes to map their positions on the chromosome (genetic map). Drosophila: life cycle about two weeks; many offspring from one mating; easy to grow on simple medium; males and females easily told apart; many visible variations (any two).

scheme.step: Recombination frequency used as distance → genetic map

hint: Genes close together on one chromosome are rarely separated by crossing over. Lower recombination means closer genes.
model_answer:
*How much to write: one line each for (i) and (ii), 3 lines for (iii) · 6 minutes*

**(i)** <mark>Linkage</mark>: genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together, so parental combinations are far more frequent than new ones (Morgan).

**(ii)** <mark>Eye colour and body colour</mark> are more tightly linked: their recombination frequency (<u>1.3%</u>) is much lower than that of eye colour and wing size (37.2%).

**(iii)** <u>Alfred Sturtevant</u> used the <mark>frequency of recombination between gene pairs as a measure of the distance between them</mark> and mapped their positions on the chromosome (genetic maps).
*Drosophila* suits genetic studies (any two): completes its life cycle in <u>about two weeks</u>; a single mating gives <u>a large number of progeny</u>; grows on simple synthetic medium; <u>clear differentiation of male and female</u>; many hereditary variations visible under a low-power microscope.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- (i) <mark>linkage</mark>
- (ii) 1.3% pair, because <u>lower recombination</u>
- (iii) recombination frequency → <mark>gene distance / map</mark>; two features of *Drosophila*
:::

**Marks are lost for:** calling it crossing over in (i); choosing the 37.2% pair in (ii).

label: PYQ-style
stem:
(a) A pure round yellow pea plant (RRYY) is crossed with a wrinkled green plant (rryy). Show the F1 and F2 generations with a Punnett square and give the F2 phenotypic ratio. [3]
(b) State the law that this cross illustrates and how a test cross on the F1 would confirm it. [2]
hint: Four kinds of F1 gametes.
model_answer:
*How much to write: about one page: a 16-box Punnett square for (a), 4 lines for (b) · 10 minutes*

**(a)** **P:** RRYY (round yellow) × rryy (wrinkled green); gametes RY and ry.
**F1:** all <mark>RrYy, round yellow</mark>.
F1 gametes (four kinds, equal numbers): <u>RY, Ry, rY, ry</u>.

**F2 (RrYy × RrYy):**

$$\footnotesize\rm\begin{array}{c|cccc} & RY & Ry & rY & ry\\\hline RY & RRYY & RRYy & RrYY & RrYy\\ Ry & RRYy & RRyy & RrYy & Rryy\\ rY & RrYY & RrYy & rrYY & rrYy\\ ry & RrYy & Rryy & rrYy & rryy\end{array}$$

F2 phenotypic ratio: <mark>9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green</mark>.

**(b)** **Law of independent assortment:** when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, <mark>segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair</mark>.
**Test cross:** F1 (RrYy) × double recessive (rryy) gives round yellow : round green : wrinkled yellow : wrinkled green in <mark>1 : 1 : 1 : 1</mark>, showing that the F1 made four kinds of gametes in equal numbers.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- F1 RrYy and the <u>four kinds of gametes</u>
- a complete <u>16-box Punnett square</u>
- <mark>9 : 3 : 3 : 1</mark> with phenotypes
- the law stated; test cross <mark>1 : 1 : 1 : 1</mark>
:::

**Marks are lost for:** stating the law of segregation instead; a Punnett square with wrong gametes; test cross with RRYY.

label: PYQ-style
stem: In snapdragon (dog flower), a true-breeding red-flowered plant (RR) is crossed with a true-breeding white-flowered plant (rr). Work out the F1 and F2 generations with phenotypic and genotypic ratios. Why does this cross not mean that the genes "blended"?
hint: F1 is neither red nor white. Self the F1 and count three kinds of flower in F2.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 8–10 lines with a Punnett square · 6 minutes*

**P:** RR (red) × rr (white) → gametes R and r

**F1:** all **Rr**, <mark>pink</mark>: neither allele is completely dominant (<u>incomplete dominance</u>).

**F2 (Rr × Rr):**

$$\begin{array}{c|cc}♀\backslash♂ & R & r\\\hline R & RR & Rr\\ r & Rr & rr\end{array}$$

RR = red, Rr = pink, rr = white.

- Phenotypic ratio: <mark>1 red : 2 pink : 1 white</mark>
- Genotypic ratio: 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr, so the <u>phenotypic and genotypic ratios are the same</u>.

**Not blending:** pure red and pure white plants <u>reappear unchanged in F2</u>. The alleles R and r stayed separate in the pink F1 and <u>segregated</u> at gamete formation; only their <u>expression</u> was intermediate.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- F1 genotype Rr and phenotype <mark>pink</mark>
- the Punnett square for Rr × Rr
- both ratios, <mark>1 : 2 : 1</mark>, and the remark that they are equal
- reappearance of red and white in F2 as the reason for no blending
:::

**Marks are lost for:** calling it co-dominance; writing a 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio; no Punnett square.

scheme.step: F2 Punnett square; 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white = genotypic ratio
Red and white reappear in F2, so alleles did not blend

label: PYQ-style
stem: A colour-blind man marries a woman with normal vision whose father was colour blind. Show the cross and state the proportion of (a) colour-blind sons, (b) colour-blind daughters and (c) carrier daughters among their children.
hint: Colour blindness is X-linked recessive. What X must the woman have received from her father?
model_answer:
*How much to write: 6–8 lines with a cross · 5 minutes*

Colour blindness is an <u>X-linked recessive</u> trait. Let $X^c$ = colour-blind allele.

- Man (colour blind): $X^cY$
- Woman: normal vision but her father was colour blind, so she received $X^c$ from him: she is a <mark>carrier, $X^cX$</mark>.

**Cross:** $X^cX \times X^cY$

$$\begin{array}{c|cc}♀\backslash♂ & X^c & Y\\\hline X^c & X^cX^c & X^cY\\ X & X^cX & XY\end{array}$$

$X^cX^c$ = colour-blind daughter; $X^cX$ = carrier daughter; $X^cY$ = colour-blind son; $XY$ = normal son.

**(a)** Colour-blind sons: <mark>50% of sons</mark> (¼ of all children).
**(b)** Colour-blind daughters: <mark>50% of daughters</mark> (¼ of all children).
**(c)** Carrier daughters: <mark>50% of daughters</mark> (¼ of all children).

:::tip Your answer must contain
- genotypes: man $X^cY$, woman <u>carrier</u> $X^cX$ (with the reason)
- the cross with all four children
- each proportion, stated <mark>among sons/daughters</mark> or of all children
:::

**Marks are lost for:** treating the woman as $XX$; writing the trait as autosomal; giving proportions without saying "of sons" or "of daughters".

scheme.step: Parental genotypes with reason woman is a carrier

stem: Which of the following is an example of pleiotropy?
hint: One gene, many effects.
model_answer: **(a) Phenylketonuria.** A single gene mutation shows several phenotypic effects (mental retardation, less hair and skin pigment).

label: PYQ-style
stem: A tall pea plant is crossed with a dwarf plant (tt) and gives 50% tall and 50% dwarf progeny. The genotype of the tall plant is:
hint: Which tall genotype can give a dwarf offspring?
model_answer: **(b) Tt.** A 1 : 1 test-cross ratio shows the tall parent was heterozygous.

label: PYQ-style
stem:
(a) Explain, with a cross, how sex is determined in humans. Why is it wrong to blame the mother for the birth of a girl? [2]
(b) Name the chromosomal abnormality and give two symptoms each of Down's syndrome, Klinefelter's syndrome and Turner's syndrome. [3]
hint: (a) XX × XY: which parent makes two kinds of gamete? (b) One is a trisomy of an autosome; the other two involve the sex chromosomes.
model_answer:
*How much to write: about one page: a cross in (a), a three-row table in (b) · 10 minutes*

**(a)** Humans show the <u>XX–XY type</u> of sex determination (male heterogamety).
- Female 44 + XX makes <u>only one kind of ovum</u>: 22 + X.
- Male 44 + XY makes <mark>two kinds of sperm in equal numbers</mark>: 22 + X and 22 + Y.

| Ovum \ Sperm | 22 + X | 22 + Y |
|---|---|---|
| **22 + X** | 44 + XX girl | 44 + XY boy |

So each child has a 50% chance of being a girl or a boy, and <mark>the sperm (the father's chromosome) decides the sex</mark>. Blaming the mother is wrong.

**(b)**

- **Down's syndrome** — <mark>trisomy of chromosome 21</mark> (47). Short stature with a small round head; furrowed tongue and partly open mouth; broad palm with a characteristic crease; retarded physical, psychomotor and mental development.
- **Klinefelter's syndrome** — <mark>47, XXY</mark> (an extra X). Overall masculine development but some feminine features such as enlarged breasts (gynaecomastia); sterile.
- **Turner's syndrome** — <mark>45, XO</mark> (one X missing). Sterile, with rudimentary ovaries; lack of secondary sexual characters.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- <u>female XX: one kind of ovum</u>, <u>male XY: two kinds of sperm</u>
- the cross and <mark>sperm decides the sex</mark>
- each disorder with its <u>karyotype</u> and two correct symptoms
:::

**Marks are lost for:** writing Klinefelter's as XXX or Turner's as XXY; saying the ovum decides the sex; giving only one symptom each.

scheme.step: Sperm decides sex, so mother not responsible

label: PYQ (2025)
stem: Which statement about sex determination is correct?
options: In birds, the homozygous pair ZZ gives a female.
In grasshoppers, the XO condition gives a male.
In humans, the XO condition gives a normal female.
In *Drosophila*, the homozygous pair XX gives a male.
hint: Which insect's males have one sex chromosome fewer?
model_answer: **(b).** Grasshopper: XX female, XO male. Birds: ZZ male, ZW female. Human XO is Turner's syndrome (a sterile female), not the normal way of fixing sex. *Drosophila*: XX female, XY male.

label: PYQ (2025)
stem: The karyotype of a person shows 22 normal pairs of autosomes and the sex chromosomes **XXY**. (a) Identify the disorder. (b) Write its symptoms. (c) Give the reason for it.
hint: 47 chromosomes; an extra X in a male.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 4 lines · 3 minutes*

**(a)** <mark>Klinefelter's syndrome</mark> (47, XXY).

**(b)** Overall <u>masculine development</u> but with feminine features such as <u>gynaecomastia</u> (breast development); the person is <u>sterile</u>.

**(c)** An <mark>extra copy of the X chromosome</mark>, caused by failure of chromosomes to separate (<u>non-disjunction</u>) during gamete formation, an aneuploidy.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- <mark>Klinefelter's syndrome</mark>, 47 XXY
- gynaecomastia, sterile
- extra X from <u>non-disjunction</u>
:::

**Marks are lost for:** confusing it with Turner's syndrome (45, XO, sterile female).

scheme.step: Extra X chromosome (XXY) due to non-disjunction/aneuploidy

label: PYQ (2025)
stem: Differentiate between (i) polygenic inheritance and pleiotropy; (ii) dominance, codominance and incomplete dominance.
hint: Count genes and traits for (i); look at the F1 phenotype for (ii).
model_answer:
*How much to write: two small tables with examples · 9 minutes*

**(i)**

| Polygenic inheritance | Pleiotropy |
|---|---|
| <u>many genes</u> control <u>one trait</u> | <u>one gene</u> affects <u>many traits</u> |
| effects are additive; environment also acts | one gene product acts in several pathways |
| e.g. <mark>human skin colour, height</mark> | e.g. <mark>phenylketonuria</mark> |

**(ii)**

| | F₁ hybrid shows | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Dominance | only the <u>dominant</u> parent's trait | tall × dwarf pea → all tall |
| Codominance | <u>both</u> parental traits side by side | <mark>AB blood group</mark> (Iᴬ Iᴮ) |
| Incomplete dominance | an <u>intermediate</u> phenotype | red × white snapdragon → <mark>pink</mark> |

:::tip Your answer must contain
- gene and trait counts for (i), with examples
- F₁ phenotype for each of the three in (ii)
- one example each
:::

**Marks are lost for:** giving sickle-cell anaemia for codominance without explanation; mixing codominance with incomplete dominance.

scheme.step: Polygenic inheritance vs pleiotropy: two points

label: PYQ (2024)
stem:
In pea, violet flower (V) is dominant over white (v) and axial position (A) over terminal (a). Three crosses gave these progeny:
(a) violet, axial × white, axial → 6/16 violet axial, 2/16 violet terminal, 6/16 white axial, 2/16 white terminal;
(b) violet, axial × white, terminal → 1/4 each of violet axial, violet terminal, white axial, white terminal;
(c) violet, axial × violet, axial → 3/4 violet axial, 1/4 white axial.
Find the genotypes of the parents in each cross.
hint: Take one character at a time: a 1 : 1 ratio is a test cross, 3 : 1 is hybrid × hybrid.
model_answer:
*How much to write: one line of reasoning per cross · 6 minutes* Take each character separately. **(a)** Colour 8 : 8 = 1 : 1 → Vv × vv. Position 12 : 4 = 3 : 1 → Aa × Aa.
Parents: VvAa × vvAa. **(b)** Colour 1 : 1 → Vv × vv. Position 1 : 1 → Aa × aa.
Parents: VvAa × vvaa (a dihybrid test cross). **(c)** Colour 3 : 1 → Vv × Vv. All axial → at least one parent is AA.
Parents: VvAA × VvAA (or VvAA × VvAa). :::tip Your answer must contain - ratios read one character at a time - (a) VvAa × vvAa - (b) VvAa × vvaa - (c) VvAA × VvAA (or VvAa) ::: **Marks are lost for:** giving phenotypes instead of genotypes; missing that both parents in (a) are Aa.

label: PYQ (2024)
stem: "In codominance, the influence of both alleles is clearly expressed in the heterozygote." Explain with the inheritance of the ABO blood groups in humans.
hint: Gene I, three alleles, sugars on the RBC surface.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 10 lines + a small table · 9 minutes*

- ABO blood groups are controlled by the gene <mark>*I*</mark>, which has <u>three alleles</u>: *Iᴬ*, *Iᴮ* and *i* (multiple allelism). A person has any two of them.
- The RBC membrane carries <u>sugar polymers</u>. *Iᴬ* and *Iᴮ* produce two slightly different sugars; *i* produces none.
- *Iᴬ* and *Iᴮ* are both <u>dominant over *i*</u>: *Iᴬ i* is group A and *Iᴮ i* is group B.
- When *Iᴬ* and *Iᴮ* are together, <mark>both express their own sugar</mark>, so the RBCs carry both A and B types: blood group <mark>AB</mark>. Neither masks the other and they do not blend: this is <u>codominance</u>.

| Genotype | Blood group |
|---|---|
| *Iᴬ Iᴬ*, *Iᴬ i* | A |
| *Iᴮ Iᴮ*, *Iᴮ i* | B |
| *Iᴬ Iᴮ* | AB |
| *i i* | O |

Three alleles give <u>six genotypes and four phenotypes</u>.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- gene *I*, three alleles
- sugars on RBC; *i* makes none
- <mark>*Iᴬ Iᴮ* → AB: both expressed</mark>
- 6 genotypes, 4 phenotypes
:::

**Marks are lost for:** calling AB an intermediate group (that would be incomplete dominance).

scheme.step: Gene I with three alleles Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i
Alleles produce different sugars on RBC; i none
Iᴬ and Iᴮ dominant over i
Iᴬ Iᴮ: both expressed = AB = codominance

label: PYQ (2023)
stem: In a pedigree, two unaffected parents (generation I) have four children: an affected daughter, an unaffected son (1), an affected son (2) and an unaffected daughter (3). Daughter 3 marries an unaffected man; they have an affected son and two unaffected daughters. (a) Is the trait dominant or recessive? Give a reason. (b) Is it autosomal or sex-linked? Give a reason. (c) Write the possible genotypes of children 1 and 3 of generation II.
hint: Affected child from unaffected parents; then look at the affected daughter's father.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 5–6 lines · 5 minutes* **(a)** Recessive: unaffected parents have affected children, so both parents must carry a hidden allele. **(b)** Autosomal: an affected daughter has an unaffected father. If the trait were X-linked recessive, her father would have to be affected. **(c)** Let A = normal, a = trait. Parents are Aa × Aa.
Child 1: AA or Aa.
Child 3: Aa (she has an affected son, so she must carry a). :::tip Your answer must contain - recessive, with the reason - autosomal, using the affected daughter - 1: AA/Aa; 3: Aa ::: **Marks are lost for:** giving a verdict without the reason; calling it X-linked because sons are affected.

scheme.step: Recessive; unaffected parents have affected offspring

label: PYQ (2023)
stem: (i) A true-breeding tall pea plant with round seeds is crossed with a dwarf plant with wrinkled seeds. Work out the cross up to the F₂ generation and give the phenotypic ratios of F₁ and F₂. (ii) State the Mendelian principle that can be derived only from such a cross.
hint: Four kinds of gametes from the F₁.
model_answer:
*How much to write: cross laid out in steps · 9 minutes* **Parents:** tall, round TTRR × dwarf, wrinkled ttrr
**Gametes:** TR and tr
**F₁:** all TtRr, tall and round (ratio: 100%) **F₁ selfed:** TtRr × TtRr
**Gametes of each:** TR, Tr, tR, tr (¼ each) **F₂ (16 combinations):** - tall, round: 9 - tall, wrinkled: 3 - dwarf, round: 3 - dwarf, wrinkled: 1 Phenotypic ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. **(ii) Law of independent assortment:** when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair. :::tip Your answer must contain - genotypes of parents, gametes, F₁ - four gamete types - 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 with phenotypes - law stated in words ::: **Marks are lost for:** writing only the ratio without the phenotypes; stating the law of segregation.
